title: Crypto and ICO investment fraud
body_md:
## The investment claim comes before the token
A blockchain transaction may be traceable, yet a confirmed transfer normally cannot be reversed by a bank. A dashboard balance is just a number the site displays; it is not proof that assets exist. Scams may use a fake exchange, a token whose insiders control supply or sale rules, a coordinated price pump, or an upfront “recovery” offer. These are different mechanisms; avoid diagnosing all crypto as fraud.

Ask **who controls your funds, what legal entity offers the service, what creates the return, and what you can independently verify**. Read withdrawal terms before any deposit. If an online acquaintance chooses the platform, promises stable high returns or asks you to send to a personal wallet, stop. Ads in respected media and celebrity photos are distribution and marketing, not due diligence. A tiny successful withdrawal may be deliberately permitted to build trust.

For a token presale or initial coin offering (ICO), inspect the documented project, token allocation, contract privileges and independent technical review if available. Even an audit cannot guarantee price or honesty. For a claimed financial firm, check the relevant regulator's register for its *actual activity*, not just a matching name. The Bank of Russia register covers specified Russian financial activities; it neither validates an overseas platform nor promises return.

A genuine volatile investment can lose money without being a scam. A legitimate exchange can also ask for identity checks under its own rules, but an unexpected demand to pay a separate “tax” to an unfamiliar wallet to unlock a balance is a strong fraud signal. Do not send extra money to test it. If harmed, preserve dates, transaction hashes and addresses privately, contact the exchange/payment provider promptly and report through the appropriate authority. Ignore unsolicited recovery agents.

widget_config.goal: Separate a verifiable investment proposition from a fake crypto platform or token pitch before sending funds.
widget_config.today_action: Before following any investment link, write down the exact legal entity, asset custody, return mechanism and applicable regulator; if any is unanswered, do not fund it.
widget_config.scope: Educational risk checks, not investment advice. US FBI/FTC examples and Russian register have distinct jurisdictions; checked 2026-10-20.

blocks.title: A presale with a locked exit
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a group promotes `orbit-seed.example`, promising a fixed monthly return. A token chart rises, but the terms omit who holds deposits and the contract gives its creator power to block sales.
blocks.analysis: The displayed chart does not establish trades or a real market. Missing custody and privileged contract controls mean you cannot price the risk; a fixed return promise compounds it. Do not deposit. Search independently for the entity, contract and applicable regulatory status.

blocks.title: A real platform with an awkward identity check
blocks.situation: Synthetic: you reach a licensed provider through a bookmark you set earlier. Its published terms say withdrawal after a large transaction may require an in-app identity review; it asks for no outside payment.
blocks.analysis: An identity review is not automatically a scam. Verify the exact legal entity and licensed activity with the relevant regulator, contact support from the independently reached site, and never send documents through a DM. A license reduces one uncertainty but does not remove market risk.

blocks.title: The token invitation
blocks.setup: Synthetic: a stranger in a hobby chat offers access to a new token and an “expert” trading site. You have not sent money.

steps.prompt: They show a rising balance screenshot. What question comes first?

choices.text: Who controls funds and what independently verifies the trading entity?
choices.consequence: You uncover that only the promoter supplies evidence.
choices.explanation: A screenshot is easy to fabricate; check ownership and authority.

choices.text: Assume a rising chart proves profit.
choices.consequence: You may mistake a controlled display for real assets.
choices.explanation: Displayed profit is not withdrawable value.

steps.prompt: A search finds a similarly named registered company. Next?

choices.text: Match exact legal entity, domain and licensed activity in the relevant register.
choices.consequence: A name match alone no longer carries the decision.
choices.explanation: A real company can be impersonated; a license has a defined scope.

choices.text: Transfer because any register match guarantees safety.
choices.consequence: The recipient may be an impersonator or offer an unlicensed product.
choices.explanation: Match the entity and activity, not just the brand.

steps.prompt: The promoter says a tiny withdrawal proved the site. What do you infer?

choices.text: Small withdrawals can be bait; pause without sending a test deposit.
choices.consequence: You keep your money while checking the claim.
choices.explanation: A controlled platform can return a little to obtain much more.

choices.text: Send a larger amount to see whether it also comes back.
choices.consequence: The test creates the very loss you are trying to avoid.
choices.explanation: Never use a larger deposit as proof.

steps.prompt: Later an unknown “recovery specialist” DMs a fee offer. Response?

choices.text: Do not pay; preserve evidence and use official reporting/provider routes.
choices.consequence: You avoid a second loss and retain useful records.
choices.explanation: IC3 warns specifically about upfront recovery offers.

choices.text: Pay because the specialist knows your transaction hash.
choices.consequence: Public ledger data can be copied by anyone.
choices.explanation: Knowing a hash proves no recovery authority.

blocks.debrief: The decisive checks are recipient, control, regulated activity and actual withdrawal terms. Risk remains even after a genuine firm is identified.

questions.prompt: A token contract has an audit badge. What follows?

choices.text: Review the audit scope; it cannot guarantee price or honesty.
choices.explanation: An audit examines defined code, not every business or market risk.
An audit does not remove market or liquidity risk.

questions.prompt: A Russian register lists a similar firm name. Best interpretation?

choices.text: Check exact identity and authorized activity; do not infer returns.
choices.explanation: The register has a defined jurisdiction and activity scope.

choices.text: Any crypto product worldwide is certified.
choices.explanation: The Russian register cannot certify the world.

questions.prompt: A platform demands a separate wallet transfer to release profits. What now?

choices.text: Stop payments, retain records and contact provider/authorities.
choices.explanation: Extra “unlock” payments are a known fraud pattern.

choices.text: Pay once because a displayed balance exceeds the fee.
choices.explanation: The displayed balance may be fiction; fees can recur.
